note: Where to learn a topic from scratch, as opposed to the per-concept readings in concepts.json. A concept reading answers 'where do I read about alignment'; a resource here answers 'where do I learn C++'.

cpp.title: Learning C++
cpp.blurb: Your notes follow learncpp.com, which is the right choice — it is free, it is ordered so nothing depends on something later, and it is unusually careful about the things that are undefined. The rest of these are references rather than courses.

resources.title: learncpp.com
resources.where: Start at chapter 0 and do not skip. You are around chapter 4-5.
resources.note: Free, complete, and the ordering is the value. Chapter 8 is control flow — loops and if — which is the next thing that unlocks most of the problems here.

resources.title: cppreference.com
resources.where: Look things up here, not on Stack Overflow
resources.note: The reference, and the closest readable thing to the standard. Hard going at first; get used to it early, because every answer you find elsewhere is a worse version of what is here.

resources.title: C++ Core Guidelines
resources.where: Skim the ES (expressions and statements) section
resources.note: Stroustrup and Sutter on what to actually do. Not a tutorial — read it once you can write a program, as a list of habits worth forming.

resources.title: Compiler Explorer
resources.where: Paste anything in and look at the assembly
resources.note: The single most educational tool for this language. Write a loop, see what -O2 does to it. This is how you find out what the compiler is really doing with your code.

resources.title: A Tour of C++
resources.where: Stroustrup — read after learncpp, not instead of it
resources.note: Short, dense, written by the language's author. It assumes you can already program, and it is the fastest way to see the whole language at once.

resources.title: Back to Basics (CppCon)
resources.where: The series, one talk per topic
resources.note: An hour per subject from people who know it well. The ones on initialisation, lifetime and the type system are worth it even after reading the chapters.

arch.title: Computer architecture
arch.blurb: One book does most of the work here, and it is the same book that covers the C side of the machine.

resources.title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
resources.note: The best single book for a programmer who wants to know what the hardware does. Chapter 6 on the memory hierarchy is the one to read first.

resources.title: Nand2Tetris
resources.where: Free, and you build a computer from gates up
resources.note: Start here if the machine still feels like magic. Twelve projects from a NAND gate to a working computer.

resources.title: Agner Fog's optimization manuals
resources.note: What real CPUs do, measured rather than documented. Reference material, not reading.

os.title: Operating systems
os.blurb: OSTEP is free, friendly and complete; TLPI is the reference for the Linux API specifically.

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
resources.note: Genuinely the best introduction, and free. Three parts: virtualisation, concurrency, persistence.

resources.title: The Linux Programming Interface
resources.note: 1500 pages and worth owning. Use it to look things up rather than to read through.

resources.title: man7.org
resources.where: The man pages, online and well formatted
resources.note: Same author as TLPI. `man 2 <syscall>` is the habit to build.

algo.title: Algorithms
algo.blurb: One free book to practise from, one reference to look things up in.

resources.title: Competitive Programmer's Handbook
resources.where: Free PDF, and the chapters are short
resources.note: Written for contests, which makes it unusually practical. The CSES problem set beside it is a good ladder.

resources.title: Introduction to Algorithms
resources.note: Not a book to read front to back. Look up the chapter you need.

resources.title: The Algorithm Design Manual
resources.note: The war stories in it are the best argument for why any of this matters.

compilers.title: Compilers and interpreters
compilers.blurb: Crafting Interpreters is free, excellent and the only one of these you should start with.

resources.title: Crafting Interpreters
resources.where: Free online, and you build two interpreters
resources.note: The clearest writing on this subject anywhere. Part I is a tree-walking interpreter; part II is a bytecode VM in C.

resources.title: Engineering a Compiler
resources.note: The textbook to use after Crafting Interpreters, and more approachable than the Dragon Book.

resources.title: LLVM Kaleidoscope tutorial
resources.where: Build a language on a real backend
resources.note: Where to go once you want your compiler to produce fast machine code rather than bytecode.

linux.title: Linux and the command line
linux.blurb: The shell rewards a few hours of deliberate study more than almost anything else.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
resources.note: Shell, scripting, git, debugging, profiling. Start here.

resources.title: Julia Evans' zines
resources.note: The friendliest explanations of hard tools that exist.

resources.title: Systems Performance
resources.where: Gregg — for when something is slow
resources.note: The methodology chapters are the valuable part: how to find out what is slow rather than guessing.

resources.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
resources.note: The best technical book of the last decade, and the one to read before any of the papers.

resources.title: MIT 6.824
resources.note: The labs build a Raft implementation. Hard, and the fastest way to actually understand consensus.

resources.title: The Raft paper
resources.where: Written to be readable, and it is
resources.note: Start with the visualisation on raft.github.io, then read the paper.

hpc.title: HPC and performance
hpc.blurb: Performance work is a skill with its own literature, and most of it is about memory.

resources.title: MIT 6.172 Performance Engineering
resources.where: Free on OCW, with lecture videos
resources.note: The best course on making real code fast. Lectures 14-15 on caching are the ones to watch first.

resources.title: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory
resources.note: Dated in places and still the definitive explanation of why memory access patterns dominate.

resources.title: Algorithms for Modern Hardware
resources.note: Modern, measured, and full of code. The closest thing to a current Drepper.

fpga.title: FPGAs and digital design
fpga.blurb: Hardware needs a different kind of practice: write HDL, simulate it, look at the waveform.

resources.title: HDLBits
resources.note: Where to actually learn to write HDL. Two hundred problems from a wire to a working FSM, checked by simulation.

resources.title: Digital Design and Computer Architecture
resources.note: The standard introduction, and it builds a RISC-V processor by the end.

resources.title: nandland
resources.note: The friendliest FPGA site there is. Good on the things textbooks skip, like clock domain crossing.

sysdesign.title: System design
sysdesign.blurb: Mostly the same book as distributed systems, plus the habit of estimating before designing.

resources.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
resources.note: Read this rather than any interview-prep book. It explains the machinery instead of listing architectures.

resources.title: The Google SRE book
resources.note: How large systems are actually operated, which is the half that design discussions usually leave out.

resources.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know
resources.note: Worth committing to memory. Every capacity estimate starts from these.
